title: Check and scaffold
description: new-integration writes a starting point. check-integration proves it works, with no service running.

Valet has a few commands for this. In Docker, run them through `docker exec valet`. From source, run them from the repo after `npm run build`.

```sh
node dist/server.js new-integration <name>
node dist/server.js new-integration <name> --full
node dist/server.js check-integration <file>
node dist/server.js config check
node dist/server.js config print
node dist/server.js config schema
```

## new-integration

```sh
docker exec valet node dist/server.js new-integration my-service
```

This writes `data/integrations/my-service.mjs`, a short `service()` that passes its own check. The name takes lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and an existing file is never overwritten.

`--full` writes the long form instead: a widget with a tile and a button, an action, a read tool and a control tool, in `my-service.mjs`, plus its own visual in `my-service.web.js`. It's commented line by line.

The file's first lines show the config block. Add that, put `my-service.status` in the layout, and restart.

## check-integration

```sh
docker exec valet node dist/server.js check-integration data/integrations/my-service.mjs
```

```text
✓ Speedbox: card, tile, assistant tool and failure handling all good
```

This runs your `service()` against the `sample` it carries, the same way Valet's own tests run every built-in. Nothing touches the real service.

It checks that:

- The config accepts the sample.
- The widget can read the sample.
- The card is valid.
- The card has a headline for small tiles.
- Each `expect` value lands where you said.
- No stat comes up empty.
- `expect` exists, so a test proves the numbers are in the right place.
- The recap says something, with no `undefined` or `NaN`, if there is one.
- The tool only reads.
- An answer of 500 fails, rather than reporting success.
- That failure doesn't show the key.

It exits non-zero if anything's wrong, so it works in a script.

Integrations written with `defineIntegration` have no sample, so it says so and skips them. Test those with `checkCard`.

## Testing against the real thing

A sample proves your code reads that answer. It can't prove the service still answers that way.

```sh
npm run test:live       # every widget in your config.yaml, against your services
npm run test:services   # service() types against your real services
```

Those are from a source checkout. They use your `.env`.

## In the repo

`npm test` validates every card sample, renders each in every size, and runs every `service()` through the same check. `npm run check` is the type check. Integration tests use made-up data only. Never commit a recorded response from a real service: they carry personal data.

## Checking a config

```sh
docker exec valet node dist/server.js config check
```

```text
✓ /config/config.yaml: 12 integrations, 18 widgets placed, assistant on
```

`config check` names every problem, and exits non-zero if there are any. An unknown key names the closest match. `config print` shows what Valet made of the file, with secrets redacted.

`config schema` prints the whole config as JSON schema, including every integration's options. Editors can use it. Save it as `valet.schema.json`, and put this at the top of your config:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=./valet.schema.json
```
